Issued at 130 PM CDT Mon Aug 3 2026

High pressure currently centered over Illinois is progged to slowly 
move east to New England by Tuesday afternoon. The ridge axis may be 
close enough to the area still tonight to allow for some patchy 
ground fog to develop, especially across rural areas of northwest 
Indiana in closer proximity to the surface ridge. Fog and low 
cloudiness isn't expected to be nearly as widespread as it was this 
morning, but opted to include some patchy fog in the grids over far 
southern and southeastern portions of the CWA. Tuesday's weather 
will be similar to today's; partly cloudy and warm with rather 
comfortable humidity levels. While there may be a lake breeze again 
Tuesday afternoon, a bit more of a southwesterly gradient should 
limit the inland extent and likely confine it to the IL shore. 

Attention will turn to the trough currently over the northern 
Rockies. This trough is expected to translate eastward across the 
northern Plains and into the upper Mississippi Valley by mid week. 
At the surface, a cold front currently across the central into the 
northern Plains will gradually move eastward in concert with the 
upper trough and into the Midwest. While high pressure to our south 
across the Gulf Coast states should limit access to Gulf moisture, 
there is a reservoir of moisture pooled ahead of this front with 
widespread dewpoints in the 70s and PWATs 1.75" to nearly 2". As the 
front settles southeastward toward our region, so too should this 
axis of richer atmospheric moisture. 

Unfortunately, there will likely be several smaller scale vorticity 
maxima embedded within the broader trough, which could complicate 
prediction of the timing and placement of better convective and 
heavy rainfall chances, especially as these small embedded 
shortwaves potentially become convectively enhanced. There is a 
signal in guidance that one such wave will support convection 
developing over the Cornbelt region Tuesday afternoon, with most 
guidance suggesting this activity could persist through the night 
and arrive in our northwestern CWA late Tuesday night/early 
Wednesday morning in a weakening state. Extensive cloud cover and 
potentially rain with this feature is expected to overspread 
especially the northern half of our area Wednesday morning with 
cloud cover and potentially showers lingering into the afternoon, 
limiting potential heating/destabilization. 

Global models are in pretty good agreement in depicting another 
embedded shortwave trough supporting more widespread convective 
development Wednesday afternoon across the southern Cornbelt/lower 
Missouri River valley. This, potentially convectively enhanced vort, 
is then expected to track eastward into Illinois Wednesday evening 
leading to an increase in coverage and intensity of rainfall. Given 
the high PWATs pooled ahead of this boundary; heavy rainfall would 
certainly be a threat, but there are a lot of moving pieces to this 
atmospheric puzzle, so forecast confidence is still on the lower end 
of the spectrum regarding where and ultimately if a heavy 
rainfall/flooding threat will materialize in our area. If a sizable 
MCS does roll across the area Wednesday night, that would likely 
push the effective surface boundary south, potentially out of our 
CWA. This could result in better rain chances Thursday ending up 
south of I-80 or potentially farther south into central Illinois. 
For now, given the lower confidence, I didn't stray from the 
aggressively high precip chances in the NBM for Thursday, but if 
confidence increases in a formidable MCS moving across the area 
Wednesday night, then the focus for redevelopment Thursday could end 
up much farther south. 

Mainly dry and seasonably warm weather is expected late in the week 
through much of the upcoming weekend. There are indications in the 
medium range guidance that we could get into a potentially more 
active northwest flow regime heading into next week with 
thunderstorm chances returning.

- Izzi
